newsitem.title: USA: Judge blocks sale of Tampa, Fla., stadium bonds.
newsitem.headline: Judge blocks sale of Tampa, Fla., stadium bonds.

text.p: A Florida judge refused Friday to validate $204.5 million of revenue bonds for the new Tampa Bay Buccaneers stadium, ruling that profit provisions in the lease served primarily a private purpose.

"This court finds that the new stadium project would serve a paramount public purpose, if not for the fact that the lease of the new stadium to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers grants the Buccaneers the first $2 million in net annual revenues from non-Bucaanner events," Circuit Judge Sam Pendino said in his ruling.

"Consequently, this court finds the stadium project to serve a predominentantly private purpose and consequently cannot validate the bonds sought to be issued by the Tampa Sports Authority," Pendino said.

Hillsbourgh County, City of Tampa and Tampa Sports Authority sought the bond validation after former Tampa Mayor Bill Poe sued to halt the tax-backed bond issue. Poe argued that the 65,000-steat stadium would unconstitutionally use public money for a project that would mainly benefit the privately owned football team.
Hillsborough County Attorney Emmeline Acton said the county and city would try to renegotiate the portion of the lease that Pendino objected to.
"He (Pendino) found 99 percent of the agreement valid except in the $2 million to the Bucs, so we will be meeting with the Bucs to see if we can renegotiate," Acton said.
"I'm very happy they found the Bucs a major economic boost, all except the $2 million. We can validate the bonds if we can negotiate the $2 million," Acton said.
Poe was subdued despite his victory, and said Pendino had done "a fair, open and fine job."

In September, voters approved a half-cent local-option sales tax to raise money for schools, public safety and the stadium. Construction began shortly after the referendum but the bond issue, to be offered via Smith Barney Inc, has been delayed by the lawsuit.

Poe's lawsuit was merged with the bond validation proceedings. During five days of testimony in the nonjury procedure earlier this month, a sports economist estimated the Bucs' annual impact on the Tampa area at $183 million.
Jack Wilson, former chairman of the Greater Tampa Chamber of Commerce, said Tampa gets valuable national publicity from the Bucs, who threatened to leave if they did not get a new stadium.

Ecnomists for the plaintiff disputed the figures. Poe's attorney, Chris Bently, said the public could end up paying at least $24 million in maintencance costs over the 30-year term of the lease because the reserve fund for maintenance will be exhausted long before the lease expires.
The contract calls for the Bucs to pay $3.5 million in annual rent for 30 years. It gives the team the first $2 million of profits from other stadium events, minus ticket sales.
